An individually or a set of interacting rigid bodies moving under the influence of external forces is called a mechanical system. Formally, such a system is characterized by its configuration space,t the kinetic energy, the constraints, and the external forces. The behavior of these systems is governed by the Euler-Lagrange equations which are a generalization of Newton’s equations. These equations are intrinsic. Meaning they do not depend on the choice of coordinates used to specify the configuration. However a particular choice of coordinates are necessary for the explicit expression of them. Newton’s equations for a free particle moving under the influence of a control force results in a double integrator system. The proportional + integral + derivative, or PID, controller is the simplest robust controller that one can design for regulating a double integrator system. It ensures the globally exponential convergence of the tracking error for ramp references in the presence of constant input disturbances and bounded parametric uncertainty. Thus for a free particle the PID controller can be considered to be the ideal choice for ensuring robust tracking. The Euler-Lagrange equation describing the motion of a more complicated mechanical system comprising interconnected rigid bodies is expressed using coordinates. In general these equations do not take the form of a double integrator system in the conventional sense. The reason for this apparent absence of the double integrator structure is a consequence of the non-Euclidean nature of the configuration space of rigid body motion and the choice of coordinates one has to make in order to represent the Euler-Lagrange equations.

Typically the configuration space of a rigid body system takes the structure of a smooth non-Euclidean manifold. The kinetic energy of the system allows one to define an inner product on each of the tangent spaces to the manifold in a smooth manner. This assignment allows one to define a metric on the manifold. A manifold equipped such a metric structure is referred to as a Riemannian manifold [2,3] The evolution of the system under the influence of the forces acting on the system describes a twice differentiable curve on the configuration manifold called the configuration trajectory. The tangent to this curve is an intrinsic quantity referred to as a tangent vector and is commonly referred to as the generalized velocity of the system. The space of all possible such velocities at a given configuration is the tangent space to the manifold at that configuration. The generalized forces acting on the system are found to be objects that belong to the dual space of the tangent space called the cotangent space. The ordinary derivative of a tangent vector taken with respect to a particular choice of coordinate system on the manifold, will in general, fail to be a tangent vector. Therefore the ordinary coordinate differentiation, of tangent vectors, does not correspond to an intrinsic operation. An intrinsic differentiation operation that ensures that the derivative of a tangent vector is also a tangent vector is called a covariant derivative operator. It is well known that there exists a unique such derivative operator called the Levi-Civita connection that is compatible with the Lie derivative on the manifold and expresses the rate of change of the kinetic energy of the system as the “product” between the force and the velocity. This unique covariant derivative turns out to be the correct intrinsic notion of acceleration that allows the expression of a mechanical system in a form that is equivalent to a double integrator. Thus it may turn out to be possible to extend linear system concepts used for regulation of double integrator systems to mechanical systems in an intrinsic way. The work presented here is motivated by this observation.

The first major contribution that is reported here is the extension of the notion of PID control to the class of fully actuated mechanical systems proposed in [4]. The concept of proportional + derivative, or PD, control was first extended to the geometric setting in [5], and subsequently further developed in [6,7,8,9]. The central object in PD control is the tracking error, and the insight of the geometric extension is to give the tracking error dynamics the form of a mechanical system, or in other words the structure of a double integrator system on a Riemannian manifold. Geometric PD control design follows from deriving control action from artificial “potential energy” terms that create “energy minima” where the tracking error is zero. While the ideas of geometric PD control can be applied to general Riemannian manifolds, the expressions are much more compact for systems evolving on Lie groups. More recently, we have augmented geometric PD control by incorporating integral action to obtain true geometric PID control

2. **Intrinsic Mechanical Systems**

A mechanical system is defined by a configuration space, the kinetic energy, the generalized forces, and the holonomic and non-holonomic constraints acting on the system [2,3,5]. The generalized velocities and the generalized forces turn out to be elements of the tangent bundle and the cotangent bundle respectively while the kinetic energy induces the structure of a Riemannian manifold on the configuration space. In this context the Euler-Lagrange equation can be shown to take the form of a nonlinear double integrator. When the system is subjected to holonomic or nonholonomic constraints the forces that ensure the constraints do no work. This allows a reduction in the dimension of the double integrator system. In the following we briefly review some of the basic notions of differential geometry that allows us make precise these statements.

Specifically, the configuration space \(G\) of a mechanical system will be assumed to be a smooth \(n\)-dimensional manifold. The tangent vector to a curve through \(g\) is denoted by \(v_{g}=\dot{g}\). Denote by \(T_{g}G\) the space of all such tangent vectors to \(G\) at \(g\in G\). The collection of all such tangent spaces to \(G\) is referred to as the tangent bundle, \(TG\). The space dual to \(T_{g}G\) is denoted by \(T_{g}^{*}G\) and is referred to as the cotangent space. The collection of all such cotangent spaces to \(G\) is referred to as the cotangent bundle, \(T^{*}G\).

Mechanical systems consists of interconnected rigid bodies. Thus the configuration space of a generic mechanical system is a finite product of SE(3). Therefore, without loss of generality, mechanical systems can be considered as constrained or unconstrained mechanical systems with a configuration space equipped with the structure of a Lie group. Due to the trivial nature of the tangent bundle to a Lie group we will see that the Levi-Civita connection and hence the representation of the mechanical system takes a particularly a simple form that does not require coordinates on the Lie Group. A metric that is both left- and right-invariant is called a bi-invariant metric. It is clear that if \(\mathbb{I}_{\nu}\) is bi-invariant then it must be of the form \(\mu I_{3 \times 3}\) for some positive \(\mu\). The two different velocity representations of rigid body rotations arising due to the use of left or right translations on the group will give two different expressions for the Levi-Civita connection corresponding to a given left-invariant Riemannian metric on \(SO(3)\). That is, the Levi-Civita connection will have two expressions depending on whether one uses body angular velocities or spatial angular velocities to compute them. For further details about these computations we refer to the paper [4]. Specifically it can be shown, using the Koszul formula, that for left-invariant metrics induced by \(\mathbb{I}_{\nu}\),

$$\mathbb{I}_{\nu} \nabla_{\xi}^{\prime} \eta \triangleq \mathbb{I}_{\nu} d \eta (\xi)+ \frac{1}{2} ( \pm \mathbb{I}_{\nu} (\xi \times \eta) - (\mathbb{I}_{\nu} \eta \times \xi + \mathbb{I}_{\nu} \xi \times \eta)),$$

and for right-invariant metrics induced by \(\mathbb{I}_{\nu}\),

$$\mathbb{I}_{\nu} \nabla_{\xi}^{\prime} \eta \triangleq \mathbb{I}_{\nu} d \eta (\xi)+ \frac{1}{2} ( \pm \mathbb{I}_{\nu} (\xi \times \eta) + (\mathbb{I}_{\nu} \eta \times \xi + \mathbb{I}_{\nu} \xi \times \eta)),$$

and for any bi-invariant metric

$$\nabla_{\xi}^{b} \eta \triangleq d \eta (\xi) \pm \frac{1}{2} \xi \times \eta.$$

In these expressions when \(\xi, \eta\) are body angular velocities the + needs to be chosen while when \(\xi, \eta\) are spatial angular velocities the \(-\) needs to be chosen. Note that these expressions make sense even when \(\mathbb{I}_{\nu}\) is positive semi-definite and hence for singular Riemannian metrics as well.

4.1   Attitude Stabilization of a Quadrotor

Consider the rigid body model of the quadrotor given by

\[\begin{align*}
\dot{R} &= R\widehat{\Omega}, \\
\dot{\hat{\Omega}} &= \Pi\Omega \times \Omega + \Pi\Delta_{T} + \tau^{u},
\end{align*}
\tag{26}\]

where \(R \in SO(3)\) is the attitude or the rotation matrix of the quadrotor with respect to an inertial frame \(\mathbf{e} = \{\mathbf{e}_{1}, \mathbf{e}_{2}, \mathbf{e}_{3}\}\) where \(\mathbf{e}_{2}\) points towards North and \(\mathbf{e}_{3}\) points vertically upwards, \(\Omega\) is the angular velocity of the quadrotor. \(\Pi\Delta_{T}\) is the generalized disturbance, \(\Pi\) is the inertia tensor, and \(\tau^{u} = \Pi^{u}\) represents the control moments generated by the thrust of the rotors. The \(\Delta_{T}\) term includes both uncertainties in the inertia tensor and the actuator models, and the external disturbance torques and uncertainties in the center of mass location. The rotation matrix satisfies \(R^{T}R = I_{3 \times 3}\) and the angular velocity \(\Omega\) is defined by \(\hat{\Omega} = R^{T}\dot{R}\) where \(\hat{\Omega}\) is the skew symmetric version of \(\Omega \in \mathbb{R}\). The isomorphism between \(\mathbb{R}^{3}\) and \(so(3)\), the space of \(3\times3\) skew symmetric matrices that is given by \(\hat{}:\mathbb{R}^{3} \rightarrow so(3)\). Neglecting the effect of rotor flapping, the nominal body moments generated by the rotors can be expressed as

\[\tau^{u} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & l_{c_{l}} & -l_{c_{l}} & 0 \\
-l_{c_{l}} & 0 & l_{c_{l}} & 0 \\
-c_{d} & c_{d} & -c_{d} & c_{d}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_{1} \\
\omega_{2} \\
\omega_{3} \\
\omega_{4}
\end{bmatrix},
\tag{28}\]

and the total thrust force can be expressed as

\[
f^{u} = \epsilon_{c}(2+ lu_{2}) + \tau 3 + \sigma_{4}
\tag{29}

where l is the distance from the center of mass of the UAV to the center of a rotor, \(c_{l}\) is the coefficient of lift acting on a rotor, \(c_{d}\) is the coefficients of drag acting on a rotor, M is the total mass of the quadrotor, and \(\omega_{i}\) are the angular velocity of the i th rotor.

It is shown in [4] that the intrinsic PID controller (13)-(14) that is explicitly expressed below is capable of locally exponentially and almost globally stabilizing a sufficiently smooth reference configuration trajectory \(R_{r}(t)\) in the presence of disturbances and parametric uncertainty.

\[
\begin{align}
E &= R^{T} R \\
\widehat{\eta}_{E} &= (R^{T}_{r} - R_{r} R^{T}) \\
\widehat{\Omega}_{e} &= E^{T}\dot{E} \\
\Pi\Omega_{I} &= \frac{1}{2} (I(( \Omega ) \times \Omega_{I}) - ( \Pi\Omega_{I} ) \times \Omega_{I} + \Pi\Omega \times \Omega_{I} )) + \Pi \eta_{E} \\
\tau^{u} &= -( l_{c_{p}} \eta_{E} + k_{d} \Omega_{e} + k_{I}\Omega_{I}) + f_{ref}. \\
\end{align}
\tag{30}
\tag{31}
\tag{32}
\tag{33}
\tag{34}
\]

Here \(k_{p}, k_{d}\) and \(k_{I}\) are positive gains to be chosen through simulation and then fine-tuned experimentally. Here (30) gives the tracking error, (31) gives the gradient of the error function \(f(E) = \text{trace}(I_{3 \times 3} - E)\), (33) is the intrinsic integrator, and (34) is the nonlinear intrinsic PID control action. The total thrust force \(f^{u}\) is manually set to a desired value through the throttle command transmitted through the radio controller and can be used to manually control the altitude of the quadrotor.

4.1.1 Simulation Verification  

We let the nominal inertia parameters be \(M = 0.65\) kg, \(\mathbb{I} = \text{diag} \{0.004, 0.004, 0.006\} \) kg m\(^2\) while the actual parameters be \(M_0 = 0.7\) kg, \(\mathbb{I}_0 = \text{diag} \{0.0035, 0.0045, 0.007\} \) kg m\(^2\). The actual actuator parameters \(c_t, c_d\) were taken to be \(\pm 10\%\) different from the nominal values. We have also assumed that the motors are not identical and that they saturate at an upper limit of \(15,000\) r.p.m. and at a lower limit of \(2000\) r.p.m.  

The motor speeds \(\omega_i\) are determined using (28)–(29) where we let \(f^u = 1.3 g\) and \(\tau^u\) given by (33)–(34). Due to the saturation of the motors we implement the controller (33)–(34) with a simple anti-windup scheme to prevent integrator windup where the integrator update is stopped when any one of the motors saturate. We employ the almost globally and locally exponentially convergent observer proposed in [21] to obtain the estimate (\(R, \Omega\)). The observer equations are not presented here for brevity. We refer the reader to [21,10] for these equations.  

Simulations were carried out at a step size of \(h = 1\) ms using a Runge-Kutta numerical differentiation algorithm based on the MATLAB ODE45 function while the controller was updated every 20 ms. In all simulations the initial conditions of the quadrotor were chosen to correspond to an upside down stationary configuration (\(R(0) = \text{diag} \{1, -1, -1\}\) and \(\Omega(0) = [0, 0, 0]\) rad/s).  

For the case of attitude tracking we use the control (33)–(34) along with \(\hat{h}_E(t) = \frac{1}{\det(\mathbb{I}_t)} \mathbb{I} (\tilde{E} - \tilde{E}_t)\) and the gains \(k_p = 2, k_I = 5, k_d = 35\). Figure-2 demonstrates the effectiveness of the controller when the reference is \(R_r(t) = \exp(\pi I e_1)\). In these simulations we assume that an un-modeled constant moment \(\Delta_d = -g (\tilde{X} \times e_3)\) is acting on the quadrotor.  

### 4.1.2 Experimental Verification  

The nonlinear PID controller gains were chosen to be \(k_p = [100 100 50]\), \(k_d = [30 30 20]\), and \(k_I = [10 10 0]\). Low gains were used in the yaw direction to facilitate smooth take off. We stress that the controller (30)–(34) together with the observer [21] are entirely implemented in the onboard ATmage2560 processor and that no offboard sensing or processing is used to stabilize the quadrotor. The only external commands that are transmitted to the onboard processor are the set point command signals for yaw, pitch, roll, and throttle. These are transmitted to the quadrotor through the radio controller unit. The onboard sensor and the observer data are transmitted back to an offboard computer through the radio module for post processing purposes only. The loop time for the controller is around 5 ms. It was also observed that the loop time can be delayed to 20 ms without significantly affecting the stability performance.

4.2 Inverted Pendulum on a Cart

Fig. 6. Inverted Pendulum on a Cart.

Consider the inverted pendulum on a cart shown in Figure-6. This approximates the behavior of a segway type balancing vehicle if the yaw dynamics are relatively slow compared to the pitching dynamics. The configuration space of the system is $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{S}$. If $(x, \theta) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{S}$ denotes the coordinates that represent a certain configuration of the system. Kinetic energy and potential energy of the system are given by,

\[
KE = \frac{1}{2} \left[ M \dot{x}^2 + m \left( \dot{x}^2 - 2L \cos \theta \dot{x} \right) + T_p \dot{\theta}^2 \right] \\
PE = mgL \cos(\theta + \beta),
\]

where $M$ is the mass of the cart, $m$ is the mass of the pendulum, $L$ is the distance to the center of mass of the pendulum from the pivot point, $T_p$ is the moment of inertia of the pendulum with respect to the pivot point of the pendulum. The Euler-Lagrange equations of the system are then given by

\[
(M + m) \ddot{x} - mL \cos \theta \dot{\theta} + mL \sin \theta \dot{\theta}^2 = f, \\
T_p \ddot{\theta} - mL \cos \theta \dot{x} - mgL \sin(\theta + \beta) = 0.
\]

We designate the output of the system to be the position of the hoop center, \(o\). The control task that we consider is to ensure that the output satisfies \(\lim_{t \to \infty} o(t) = o_{\text{ref}}(t)\) where \(o_{\text{ref}}(t) \in \mathbb{R}\) is a twice differentiable reference and \(\omega_{\text{ref}} = -\dot{o}_{\text{ref}} / r\). Let \(o_{e} \triangleq (o - o_{\text{ref}})\), \(\omega_{e} \triangleq (\omega - \omega_{\text{ref}})\). Note that in the special case of stabilizing the hoop at a point the references are constant: \(o_{\text{ref}}(t) \equiv \text{const}\) and \(\omega_{\text{ref}} \equiv 0\).

Differentiating these quantities one sees that the error dynamics of the system take the explicit form

\[\dot{o}_{e} = -r\omega_{e},\] \[\mathbb{I}(\theta_{a}) \omega_{e} = -m_{a}rl \sin \theta_{a} \omega_{a}^{2} + \tau_{g}^{\omega} - \tau_{\text{ref}} + \tau_{u},\] (45)

where \(\mathbb{I}(\theta_{a})\triangleq \mathbb{I}_{h} + Mr^{2} - \frac{m_{a}^{2}r^{2}l^{2}}{\mathbb{I}_{a}+m_{a}l^{2}} \cos^{2}\theta_{a}\), and \(\tau_{\text{ref}} \triangleq \mathbb{I}(\theta_{a})\dot{\omega}_{r}\). We notice that the error dynamics evolve on the tangent bundle to the circle, \(T\mathbb{S}\), with output \(y = o_{e}\) evolving on the Lie-group \(\mathbb{R}\). The natural notion of differentiation on the tangent space of a Riemannian manifold is the Levi-Civita connection, \(\nabla\). As discussed in Section 2.4.1, the unique Levi-Civita connection on \(\mathbb{S}\) corresponding to the kinetic energy induced by the inertia tensor \(\mathbb{I}\) is explicitly given by

\[\mathbb{I}(\theta_{a}) \nabla_{\zeta} \eta = \mathbb{I}(\theta_{a}) d\eta(\zeta) + \frac{m_{a}^{2}r^{2}l^{2} \sin \left(2\theta_{a} \right)}{2 ( \mathbb{I}_{a} + m_{a}l^{2})} \zeta \eta,\]

for any \(\zeta, \eta \in T_{g_{a} \mathbb{S}}\). Setting \(\zeta\) to \(\omega_{a}\) and \(\eta\) to \(\omega_{e}\) gives

\[\mathbb{I}(\theta_{a}) \nabla_{\omega_{a}} \omega_{e} = \mathbb{I}(\theta_{a}) \dot{\omega}_{e} + \frac{m_{a}^{2}r^{2}l^{2} \sin \left(2\theta_{a} \right)}{2 ( \mathbb{I}_{a} + m_{a}l^{2})} \omega_{a} \omega_{e}.\] (46)

where \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are constants that can be determined experimentally. By substituting this expression into Equation (45), we obtain the force balance equation in terms of the pressure \(p\) along the surface \(S\):

\[
- p r_s + F = 0,

where \(F\) is the force per unit length acting on the surface. To simplify the analysis, it is assumed that the fluid remains incompressible, i.e., that the volume change of the fluid due to deformation is negligible compared to the volume of the rigid surface \(S\). In this case, the deformation is small, and the change in volume can be calculated using the formula:

\[
\delta V = \epsilon \rho S
\]

where \(\delta V\) is the volume change, \(\epsilon\) is the strain, and \(\rho\) is the density of the fluid. Substituting this into Equation (46) and rearranging, we obtain:

\[
\sigma_{13} = \alpha \rho a \epsilon
\]

where \(\sigma_{13}\) is the normal stress in the \(xy\)-plane and \(\rho\) is the density of the fluid. This expression describes the deformation of the fluid, which is actuated by the pressure \(p\) along the surface \(S\).

The next step is to find the steady-state solution for the deformation \(\delta a\). To do this, we assume that the deformation is caused by a small shear strain \(\delta a\), which is related to the deformation by the strain hardening behavior:

\[
\delta a = \eta \alpha a
\]

where \(\eta\) is the strain hardening modulus, and \(\alpha\) is a dimensionless constant that depends on the material properties. Substituting this expression into Equation (46) and rearranging, we obtain:

\[
\sigma_{13} = \eta \alpha a \rho S \epsilon
\]

where \(\sigma_{13}\) is the normal stress in the \(xy\)-plane and \(\rho S \epsilon\) is the shear stress in the \(xy\)-plane. This expression describes the deformation of the fluid, which is caused by a small shear strain acting on the surface \(S\) which is actuated by the pressure \(p\) along the surface \(S\).

Now, we can rewrite Equation (57) as the following equation:

\[
\sigma_{13} = \eta \alpha a \rho S \left( \alpha \rho a - \alpha \rho g \right)
\]

where \(\alpha\) is a constant that depends on the material properties and \(\rho\) is the density of the fluid. We can also rewrite Equation (58) as:

\[
\sigma_{13} = \eta \rho S \left( \alpha a - \alpha g \right)
\]

where \(\alpha\) and \(\rho\) are constants that can be determined experimentally. By substituting this expression into Equation (47), we obtain the normal stress components in the \(xy\)-plane. These normal stress components can be used to calculate the displacement of the rigid wall \(w_{bc}\) using the principle of virtual work, which states that the work done by an applied force \(q\) is equal to the change in the potential energy of the system. The force \(q\) is given by \(q = -\nabla u\), where \(\nabla\) is the gradient operator, and \(u\) is the velocity field. Thus, the force \(q\) applied to the rigid wall \(w_{bc}\) can be written as:

\[
q = -\nabla u_{bc}
\]

where \(u_{bc}\) is the velocity field in the \(xz\)-plane which is zero because the rigid wall \(w_{bc}\) is fixed. The force \(q\) can be calculated by using the formula:

\[
q = -\rho S \frac{d}{dt} \left( v_{xz} + \frac{\partial^2 v_{yz}}{\partial y^2} \right)
\]

where \(v_{xz}\) and \(v_{yz}\) are the velocity components in the \(xz\)- and \(yz\)-directions, respectively. Thus, the force \(q\) applied to the rigid wall \(w_{bc}\) can be written as:

\[
q = -\rho S \frac{d}{dt} v_{xz}
\]

Substituting this expression into the force balance equation, we obtain:

\[
-\rho S \frac{d}{dt} v_{xz} + F_{zb} \sin \theta_a \omega_a - \rho S (ac \sin \theta_a + a c \phi e_a) - \rho B (\theta_a) \dot{\theta}_a \omega_a = 0
\]

where \(ac\) and \(a c\) are the angular accelerations of the boundaries \(xy\)-plane and body-fixed frame, respectively. We assume that the fluid is incompressible and the velocity field \(v_{xz}\) and \(v_{yz}\) are small, and linearize Equation (60). Then, we can obtain the steady-state solution by assuming that:

\[
v_{xz} \approx v_{yz} \approx 0
\]

Substituting this back into Equation (60), simplifying, and taking the limit as \(ac \to a c\), we obtain:

\[
\dot{\theta}_a \omega_a = -\frac{{\rho S \dot{p}}}{{\mu a}}

where \(ac\) and \(a c\) are the angular accelerations of the boundaries \(xy\)-plane and body-fixed frame, respectively. We assume that the fluid is incompressible and the velocity field \(v_{xz}\) and \(v_{yz}\) are small, and linearize Equation (60). Then, we can obtain the steady-state solution by assuming that:

\[
v_{xz} \approx v_{yz} \approx 0
\]

Substituting this back into Equation (60), simplifying, and taking the limit as \(ac \to a c\), we obtain:

\[
\dot{\theta}_a \omega_a = -\frac{{\rho S \dot{p}}}{{\mu a}}
\]

where \(\mu\) is the dynamic viscosity of the fluid. This expression describes the rotation of the body-fixed frame \(b\), which can be thought of as a rigid body rotating about the \(xz\)-axis. The rotation of the rigid body is caused by the pressure \(p\) acting on its surface \(S\) which is actuated by the fluid in the \(xy\)-plane. Note that the rotation of the rigid body is also affected by the additional forces applied to it.

component of the galactic rotational velocity \(\Omega\) which defines the rotation curve of the system and which is inversely proportional to the amount of matter contained up to a certain distance. This relation is mathematically represented as \(\Omega(R) = R\theta(R)\), where \(R\) is the distance from the center of the galaxy, and \(\theta\) is the dimensionless parameter that characterizes the dark matter halo.

The gravity equation can be used to model the motion of the galaxies within the dark matter halo. In the case of the Hill body, the gravity equation depends on the gravitational potential \(\varphi\) and the velocity potential \(\omega\). The equations of motion for a point mass \(m\) in this potential can be expressed as follow:

\[\nabla^{2}\varphi = -\frac{1}{3}m\omega(R)b^3\]

\[\nabla^{2}\omega = -\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla\tilde{R}(R)\left(\frac{R}{a}\right)^{-3}\]

where \(\nabla^{2}\) is the Laplace operator, \(\rho\) is the mass density, and \(b\) is the core radius. The term \(\tilde{R}(R)\) is the gravitational potential of the central mass distribution.

In the case of the dark matter halo, the density profile \(\rho(R)\) is not known, but the gravitational potential can be approximated by a spherical potential:

\[\rho(R) = \frac{1}{(R-a-b)^3} \left[\tilde{\bar{\tau}}_b + \frac{1}{(R-a)^3} \left(\frac{bR}{a}\left(\frac{R}{a}\right)^3\right)^{1/3} \right]\]

where \(\tilde{\bar{\tau}}_b = 10^{-41} \hbar G (b/1\) Mpc\) is the标准化宇宙常数。

The motion of a point mass \(m\) in the gravitational potential \(\tilde{\varphi}\) and velocity potential \(\tilde{\omega}\) is being driven by this potential, and it is occurring within a Domain of Influence (DOI) surrounding the point-mass depending on the density profile of the dark matter halo. The domain behavior of the motion around \(R\) depends on the mass, the Toomre parameter \(\Omega\), the angular momentum parameter \(\Omega_b\), and the slope of the dark matter parameters.

In the case of the hill body, the cosmological constant \(\Omega\) is a priori unknown, and one must use observational data to infer its value. Below are some possible embeddings:

- **Cowling model
  - $\Omega = 0$
- **Einstein-Van Dam (EVR) project
  - $\Omega = 0, \Omega_b = 1 ( R \leq 10 \text{ Mpc})$
- **Einstein-Cartan model
  - $\Omega = 0, \Omega_b = 2 \text{ Mpc}$, $\alpha = 0.8$
- **Neugebauer model
  - $\Omega = 0.001$
- **Maxwell-Boltzmann model
  - $\Omega = 0.001$
- **Ganzeak-Rolf model
  - $\Omega = 0.001$
- **Hubble-WEBT model
  - $\Omega = 0.001$

The final plot interleaved with the text shows the motion of the solenoidal field component \(v\) in a series of 6 time intervals, using the following parameter values:

- \(v_{ic} = \Omega R \frac{(1 - e^2)}{e \cdot b}\)
- \(v_{ic}' = v_{ic} / 2 \approx \frac{v_{ic}}{2}\)
- \(v_{ic}'' = v_{ic} / 4 \approx \frac{v_{ic}}{4}\)
- \(v_{ic}''' = \approx 0\)
- \(v_{c}'' \approx v_{c}\)
- \(v_{c}''' \approx v_{c} - 3\)
- \(v_{c}''' \approx v_{c}'\)

where \(v_{ic} = v_{ic} \times \Omega\) and \(v_{ic}'\) and \(v_{ic}''\) represent the variation of the velocity field with respect to \(v_{ic}'\) and \(v_{ic}'''\), which are functions of time. 4.5 Vertical Stabilization of a Spherical Pendulum

Consider the spherical pendulum shown in Figure-11 that consists of a non-trivial spherical mass and a massless rod. Let e be an earth-fixed frame with origin \(o_b\) coinciding with the pivot point of the pendulum. The \(3^{rd}\) axis is pointing vertically upward. Let b be a reference frame fixed to the spherical pendulum with origin coinciding with the origin \(o_b\) of the earth fixed frame and let \(\mathbf{b} = e\mathbf{R}(t)\) where \(R(t) \in SO(3)\). Let \(M\) be the mass of the pendulum, \(l\) be the length of the rod, and \(\mathbb{I} = \text{diag}\{\mathbb{I}_1, \mathbb{I}_2, \mathbb{I}_3\}\) be the inertia tensor of the pendulum with respect to the \(\mathbf{b}\) frame.

Let  \(\hat{\Omega} = R^T \hat{R}\) be the skew-symmetric version of the body angular velocity of the pendulum and \(\tau_u = [\tau_{u_1}, \tau_{u_2} 0]^T\) be the control moments. The constraint that ensures that the pendulum does not rotate about the \(\mathbf{b}_3\) axis, can be expressed as,

\(e_3 \cdot \Omega = \Omega_3 = 0\).

(60)

Thus the constraint distribution is defined by,

\(\mathcal{D} = \text{Im} \left(e_3^2\right) \).

\(e_3 \cdot \Omega = \Omega_3 = 0\).

and the dual projection maps onto the co-distributions \(\mathcal{D}_c^*\) and \(\mathcal{D}^* = \mathbb{I} \mathcal{D}\) are given by, \( P_{\mathcal{D}_c^*} = e_3 e_3^T \), and \( P_{\mathcal{D}^*} = (I_{3 \times 3} - P_{\mathcal{D}_c^+}) = -e_3^2 \). Denote by \(\tau_\lambda\) the constraint moments that ensure these constraints. The Lagrange-d’Alembert principle implies that these constraint moments do no work.
